knowledge_point.title: Integrating Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions With Linear Arguments

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=x - \frac{\pi}{6},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ | $\frac{2 \pi}{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}} 2\csc(x - \frac{\pi}{6})\cot(x - \frac{\pi}{6})\,\text{d}x & =\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 2\csc(u)\cot(u)\,\text{d}u \\ & =2\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \csc(u)\cot(u)\,\text{d}u \\ & =-2\csc(u)\big|_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =-2(\csc(\frac{\pi}{2})-\csc(\frac{\pi}{3})) \\ & =-2(1-\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3}) \\ & =-2 + \frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=4 x - \frac{\pi}{4},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi}{8}$ | $\frac{3 \pi}{16}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi}{4}$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{8}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{16}} 6\csc(4 x - \frac{\pi}{4})\cot(4 x - \frac{\pi}{4})\,\text{d}x & =\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 6\csc(u)\cot(u)\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{3}{2}\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \csc(u)\cot(u)\,\text{d}u \\ & =- \frac{3}{2}\csc(u)\big|_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =- \frac{3}{2}(\csc(\frac{\pi}{2})-\csc(\frac{\pi}{4})) \\ & =- \frac{3}{2}(1-\sqrt{2}) \\ & =- \frac{3}{2} + \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=4 x - \frac{\pi}{3},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives 

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{7 \pi}{48}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $- \frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{\pi}{4}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{0}^{\frac{7 \pi}{48}} 2\sec(4 x - \frac{\pi}{3})\tan(4 x - \frac{\pi}{3})\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int_{- \frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sec(u)\tan(u)\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\sec(u)\big|_{- \frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}(\sec(\frac{\pi}{4})-(\sec(- \frac{\pi}{3}))) \\ & =-1 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=4 x + \frac{\pi}{3},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $- \frac{\pi}{24}$ | $\frac{\pi}{24}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{- \frac{\pi}{24}}^{\frac{\pi}{24}} \csc(4 x + \frac{\pi}{3})\cot(4 x + \frac{\pi}{3})\,\text{d}x & =\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \csc(u)\cot(u)\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \csc(u)\cot(u)\,\text{d}u \\ & =- \frac{1}{4}\csc(u)\big|_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =- \frac{1}{4}(\csc(\frac{\pi}{2})-\csc(\frac{\pi}{6})) \\ & =- \frac{1}{4}(1-2) \\ & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=3 x - \frac{\pi}{4},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi}{12}$ | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{4}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 3\sec^{2}(3 x - \frac{\pi}{4})\,\text{d}x & =\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sec^{2}(u)\,\text{d}u \\ & =\tan(u)\big|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ & =(1-(0)) \\ & =1\end{aligned}
$$
